title: Pay with Kid Thomas and all-night work for a dollar
summary: He made more money with Thomas than any band, out-of-town work for $8 to $10 before the union; elsewhere he played all night for a dollar.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: I usually get up around that time anyway.
I was going to ask some more. You were talking about these bands like working with Kid Thomas. You might as well go on from there. Is there anything else you want to continue along that line?

Well, yeah, like I said, I played with Thomas. I made more money with him than any band I played with. How kind of money did you make? Did Kips, you mean? Well, in average it was more money but less money. You see, the skills wasn't like it is now. We wasn't in the union. And we was making around $8 and $10 going out of town. That's why we was getting more out of town work, you see. And we played the jobs around there in town. Some of them wasn't paying but a dollar and a dollar and a quarter a night. Two dollars. Two and a half and you made two dollars right there, you was making big money. So that's why we used to grab for all the out of town works. And Thomas had built up a nice reputation.
Was that in the Depression or during the war or before the war? Well, that was... When you were paying a dollar and a dollar and a half an hour, it must have been Depression, but it did.

Not an hour. Man, I played all night. I played all night at the Popeye for a dollar. Oh, really? People be going to work down there at 8 o'clock at night and people be going to work. 6 o'clock in the morning. We'd be playing. Balls stand on the back and say, there'll come a whole lot of people. People be going to work, wouldn't be starting about the night light. And he'd think that there's coming into the place. Come on, hear the tune, hear the tune. We'd talk to battle and oh, man. I played with Octave Crosby out there on Drys Street. They had a dance hall out there on Drys between Melphamine and Texaco. We played there, oh God knows how many years, a dollar and a quarter night, but a dollar and a quarter and a kiddie. Your kiddie would run sometime $5 and $6 a man. That's where you'd make it up. But at the actual price, what we were playing, it was sad. I was glad when the union come about so we could get in the union and get, you know, a fair price. Of course, the union scale was down a long time too before they came up to the mark that there is now. The union scale, when they first started there, was a dollar an hour. Well, you'd play four hours, you still wouldn't make the $4. So it was a long time before the bracket got up where we could get anything. Now, funerals, we used to play funerals, we'd get two and a half to three dollars was topped. We played carnival parade from six o'clock. I played carnival parade for Eleanor Club from six o'clock in the morning to six o'clock in the evening. Didn't make for $10. See, them was the bad times, but the good times, like I say, it was less money but more money. Why I said more money? Because we had more work. You was working more regularly. You know, we had more places. All the little bill gardens and things had four and five piece bands on them. And a couple of those white places was running every night. Well, that told musicians, you know, to have a little something to do. Now, me and Dude and Octave and Drum Player worked out there on Drive Street for a number of years. We used to make a dollar and a quarter of a night, but we made nice tips. Then I played with Dude's Brothers Band, Foster Lewis. He had a band and we used to travel around on percentage. Going all out through Mississippi, Moss Point, Pickyune, Laurel, Lumberton, Hazelwood, Crystal Springs, Hatterboy. He was covering that territory, Burgaloo, but go all played, but it was on percentage. Sometimes what we'd make good on this job and make three or four jobs would be so bad, it would eat up all the expense. Make a trip sometime, I'd go away and stay away a week or two weeks. Come back home maybe with a dollar, a dollar and a half, sometimes nothing. So I decided I would just give up that kind of travel and I said it don't make sense just going around playing to be playing and then getting nothing out of it. Which at that time, things, everybody mostly, you know, smaller bands was traveling around the road on percentage like that, trying to see what they could pick up. And I used to go over the lake with Gus Metcalfe every fall and play those fairs, play the Franklinton Fair and the Covington Fair. Well, that would be a nice pick up. They'd pay you $10 a day and blow it a large on that. Well, that used to, you know, mean something to us. Trying to think of some other band I worked around with.
